title: Staff counted three ways against City money
question: When City money to an organization climbed, did the number of people working there climb too, and is there enough staff on the books to do what the City pays for?
finding: Of 410 City-paid nonprofits with payroll counts on their tax returns (276 also file a staff benefit-plan return), 13 saw City payments rise by a quarter or more while their payroll count fell by a tenth or more; the largest is Catholic Charities, where City payments went from $20.7 million to $33.4 million as the payroll count went from 602 to 537. 10 organizations paid $1 million or more a year have fewer than one person on payroll for every $250,000 of City money, led by Reality House West, Inc with 1 on payroll and $3.6 million from the City; the middle organization of that size receives $42,240 per person.
how: Payroll count is line 5 of the organization's federal tax return (wage statements issued for the calendar year). Pay and benefits is line 15 of the same return. Benefit-plan count is the largest number of active participants in any one plan the organization filed with the federal labor department for the same calendar year. City money is everything the City paid in the fiscal year matching the tax period. For the first pattern the first and last years with at least $250,000 in City payments and ten or more staff are compared, at least two years apart, and only where City money is at least a fifth of the organization's spending; for the second, the latest return with $1 million or more in City payments. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. A rise in City money is counted only where the test is met on both of the Controller's tables, the nonprofit-spending table and the table of every payment, because where the two part it is not always established which is right.
limits: Neither count is full-time staff. The payroll count includes anyone paid for even a day, such as stipended youth or seasonal workers, so it can swing widely; plan counts cover only people who joined a plan. Organizations that use a staffing firm, a parent body or a union plan will not match. Falling staff with rising money can mean more subcontracting, pass-through grants or rent subsidies paid on to landlords, or a building purchase. City fiscal years and tax years overlap only roughly. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. For the 444 organizations profiled, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $210.5 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (11 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. 3 organizations met the test of money up and payroll down on one of the Controller's tables only (2 on the table of every payment, 1 on the nonprofit-spending table) and are not listed for it.
